Introduction:
In sub-Saharan Africa, the burdens of Plasmodium falciparum malaria, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and reproductive tract infections (RTIs) are among the highest globally. Each year, an estimated 12.4 million pregnant women are exposed to malaria infection [ 1 ] and 3 million are diagnosed with an STI or RTI [ 2 ]. Most STIs/RTIs are asymptomatic, and go undetected and untreated, yet can trigger inflammation that can increase stillbirth, preterm delivery, and low birthweight (LBW) risk [ 3 ]. To prevent malaria in pregnancy, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends monthly intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (SP) starting in the second trimester of pregnancy [ 4 ]. No comparable intervention exists for STIs/RTIs. In sub-Saharan Africa, the WHO recommends routine screening for syphilis and HIV, while other STIs/RTIs are managed syndromically [ 5 ], potentially missing 40%–70% of the infections [ 6 ].

Over the past two decades, the spread of P. falciparum resistance to SP in Africa [ 7 ] has motivated efforts to identify alternative IPTp regimens. Dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine (DP) is the leading candidate, given its potent antimalarial activity. In a recent meta-analysis [ 8 ], IPTp-DP was markedly more effective than IPTp-SP at preventing malaria, yet it did not yield superior birth outcomes. This unexpected finding raised the possibility that SP confers non-malarial benefits. Several observational studies support this hypothesis, suggesting a dose–response relationship between increased IPTp-SP doses and lower LBW risk, even in areas with very low malaria transmission [ 9 , 10 ] or high-level P. falciparum resistance to SP [ 11 ].

One possible non-malarial mechanism of SP is through its potential activity against STIs/RTIs [ 12 ]. The sulfadoxine component of SP belongs to the sulfonamide class of antibiotics, which have shown in vitro activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae , Chlamydia trachomatis , and Group B Streptococcus (GBS) [ 13–16 ]. Historically, sulfonamides were used to treat N. gonorrhoeae [ 17 , 18 ] and C. trachomatis [ 19 ], but were abandoned following the rapid emergence of resistance. Triple-sulfa vaginal cream was evaluated for bacterial vaginosis (BV) in the 1990s, but showed inferior cure rates compared with metronidazole [ 20 ]. Pyrimethamine has also been shown to inhibit Gardnerella vaginalis —a key organism implicated in BV [ 21 ]. While sulfonamides are no longer used clinically for STIs/RTIs and contemporary resistance patterns are not well characterized, these findings suggest the possible activity of SP against select STIs/RTIs.

In a recent randomized–controlled trial of IPTp among pregnant women from Kenya, Malawi, and Tanzania, monthly IPTp-SP reduced the C. trachomatis prevalence by 76% compared with IPTp-DP, despite IPTp-DP demonstrating superior malaria protection [ 3 ]. However, the trial did not assess GBS, despite prior in vitro evidence suggesting intermediate activity [ 13 ]. In light of this evidence, we hypothesized that IPTp-SP would be associated with reduced risks of STIs/RTIs and, consequently, improved birth outcomes. To evaluate this, we conducted a secondary analysis of a randomized–controlled trial of pregnant women that compared IPTp with SP, DP, or a combination of DP and SP (DP+SP).
Methods:
### Study population and design

We conducted a secondary analysis of a three-arm, double-blinded, placebo-controlled randomized–controlled trial (NCT04336189) that compared monthly IPTp with SP, DP, or DP+SP for the prevention of adverse birth outcomes [ 22 ]. The trial was conducted in Busia, Uganda—an area of intense, perennial malaria transmission.

Between December 2020 and December 2023, 2757 participants were enrolled. Eligibility criteria included: age ≥16 years, HIV-negative status, viable singleton pregnancy at between 12 and 20 gestational weeks confirmed by ultrasound, and agreement to receive antenatal care and deliver at the study clinic. Participants were excluded if they reported a history of serious adverse events to study drugs or had previously received IPTp-SP in their current pregnancy. We further restricted our analyses to participants who had had a vaginal swab collected.

Intervention randomization was conducted at a 1:1:1 ratio. Study drugs were initiated at 16 or 20 gestational weeks, depending on the gestational age at enrollment, and administered every 4 weeks until delivery. SP was administered as a single dose consisting of three tablets containing 500 mg of sulfadoxine and 25 mg pyrimethamine (Kamsidar, Kampala Pharmaceutical Industries). DP was administered as three consecutive daily doses; each dose consisted of three tablets containing 40 mg of dihydroartemisinin and 320 mg of piperaquine (Duo-Cotexcin, Holley-Cotec). The first dose of the study drugs was directly observed; the second and third were taken at home. Placebo pills were given to ensure that all participants received the same number and color of tablets for each IPTp course.

### Study procedures

At enrollment, participants underwent a standardized examination, were tested for syphilis and, if positive, treated with penicillin. Home visits were conducted to collect baseline data on household characteristics and malaria-prevention measures. Routine antenatal care visits were scheduled every 4 weeks for IPTp administration, clinical assessment, and blood collection. Symptomatic STIs/RTIs were managed according to national guidelines.

At delivery, standardized procedures were used to document the delivery details, collect vaginal swabs, and assess newborn outcomes. Participants were strongly encouraged to deliver at the hospital adjacent to the study clinic; those delivering elsewhere were visited by study staff at or shortly after delivery. Swabs were rotated against the vaginal wall two to three times, rolled onto microscope slides to perform Nugent scoring for BV, and placed into an Xpert® Vaginal/Endocervical Specimen Collection Kit (SWAB/A-50, Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) for storage at –80°C. Per protocol, swabs were collected at delivery. When this was not possible due to active labor or delivery outside of the study clinic, swabs were obtained at the earliest postpartum visit (1 week post-delivery) or when swab collection could be performed safely and comfortably [ 22 ]. Additional details of the study procedures are provided in Supplementary Materials Section 2 and elsewhere [ 22 ].

### STI/RTI diagnosis

Vaginal swabs were tested for C. trachomatis , N. gonorrhoeae , T. vaginalis , and GBS by using GeneXpert qPCR (Xpert® CT/NG, Xpert® TV, and Xpert® Xpress GBS; Cepheid). Due to budgetary constraints, GBS testing was discontinued midway through the trial. BV was defined as a Nugent score of 7–10, assessed by trained, blinded microscopists [ 23 , 24 ].

### Birth outcomes

Birth outcomes included: preterm delivery (<37 gestational weeks), LBW (birthweight <2500 grams), term LBW (LBW among term infants), and small-for-gestational age (SGA; <10th percentile of birthweight-for-gestational age based on INTERGROWTH-21st standards [ 25 ]. Preterm delivery included live births and fetal losses (i.e. stillbirths and miscarriages). Due to missing birthweights for fetal losses, the LBW- and SGA-based outcomes only included live births. Stillbirths and miscarriages were rare (<2%) and not separately evaluated.

### Covariates

We used a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to guide our decisions on covariate adjustment ( Fig. 1 ). Maternal age, mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), weight, and gravidity at enrollment were modeled as continuous variables. Maternal education was categorized into three levels and household-wealth tertiles were derived by using principal components analysis of common household items [ 26 ]. Current/recent alcohol use and history of any adverse delivery outcome (preterm delivery, miscarriage, or stillbirth) were assessed as binary variables at enrollment.

### Statistical analysis

This study had three objectives: (i) to compare the prevalence of STIs/RTIs between IPTp arms, (ii) to estimate associations between STIs/RTIs and adverse birth outcomes, and (iii) for STIs/RTIs associated with both IPTp-SP and adverse birth outcomes, quantify the extent to which the effects of IPTp-SP on birth outcomes are mediated through STI/RTI prevention. For Objective (i), we conducted intention-to-treat analyses by using randomized IPTp assignment. IPTp-DP served as the reference arm, assuming that DP has no antibacterial activity, and was compared with the IPTp-SP, IPTp-SP+DP, and combined IPTp-SP and IPTp-SP+DP arms. Unadjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated by using log-binomial regression. Prevalence differences and numbers needed to treat (NNT) were computed by using the Stata ‘margins’ command. Differences in the distribution of IPTp courses across the study arms were assessed by using the Kruskal–Wallis test.

To determine the associations between STIs/RTIs and adverse birth outcomes, we fitted multivariable Poisson regression models with robust standard errors, adjusting for the IPTp arm, household wealth, maternal age, weight, MUAC, education, current/recent alcohol use, history of adverse delivery outcome, and gravidity. Continuous variables were modeled as three-knot restricted cubic splines.

We used causal mediation analyses to estimate the effect of IPTp-SP on birth outcomes mediated through STI/RTI prevention. Analyses were conducted via the ‘CMAverse’ R package [ 27 ] using the parametric g-formula [ 28 ]. To ensure that the mediation analyses focused on biologically and statistically plausible pathways, analyses were limited to STI/RTIs that demonstrated associations with IPTp-SP and the birth outcome of interest. These decisions were guided by the magnitude of the estimated effects, supported by 95% CIs that excluded the null. Logistic regression was used for mediator and outcome models, and included an exposure–mediator interaction term, regardless of a statistically significant interaction [ 29 ]. We report the total (overall) effect and the natural indirect (mediated) and direct (non-mediated) effects. Mediation analyses excluded the IPTp-DP+SP arm to ensure that the comparisons were not affected by drug–drug interactions [ 30 ]. Percentile bootstrapped 95% CIs were computed based on 1000 simulations.

Analyses were performed by using Stata 16.1 (Stata Corp, College Station, Texas) and R (version 4.4.0, R Project for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

### Sensitivity analyses

Several sensitivity analyses were conducted. First, although it was intended that vaginal swabs would be collected at delivery, 28% ( n = 705) were obtained at delivery, 59% ( n = 1509) were obtained postpartum, and 13% ( n = 324) were missing or of unknown timing. The participant characteristics differed between samples collected at delivery vs postpartum ( Supplementary Material Section 1 ). To account for potential bias, we treated nondelivery samples as missing and performed multiple imputation (MI) by using chained equations with the ‘MISL’ R package [ 31 ], which employs an ensemble machine-learning approach (SuperLearner) for flexible model estimation. Imputed estimates were combined by using Rubin’s combining rules [ 32 ]. As an additional approach, inverse probability of selection weighting (IPSW) was used. Further methodological details are provided in Supplementary Material Section 2 .

Second, causal interpretation of the estimated effects assumes no unmeasured confounding. While randomization supports this assumption for estimating the effects of IPTp-SP, it may not hold for STI/RTI–birth outcome associations and mediation analyses. We therefore report E-values [ 27 , 33 , 34 ] to quantify the minimum strength that an unmeasured confounder would need to have with both the exposure and the outcome, conditional on measured covariates, to fully explain the observed effects.

Third, as fetal losses may involve different pathophysiological pathways compared with live births, we repeated STI/RTI-preterm analysis outcomes restricting to live births.
Results:
Among the 2757 participants enrolled in the parent trial, 2538 (92%) were followed to delivery and 2265 (82%) had a vaginal swab collected ( Fig. 2 ). Of these 2265 swabs, 705 (31%) were collected before delivery, 1509 (66.7%) were collected postpartum, and, for 51 (2.3%) the time of collection was unknown. Among the postpartum samples, the mean time from delivery to collection was 28 days (SD = 5). The mean age at enrollment was 24.7 years (SD = 6.3), 96% completed primary school, and 8.5% reported a prior adverse delivery outcome. Fourteen participants (0.6%) tested positive for syphilis at enrollment. Baseline characteristics were balanced across the IPTp arms ( Table 1 ). The number of IPTp courses received was comparable across the arms (median = 6 in all arms; P = .46) and compliance was high ( Supplementary Material Section 3 ).

### Effect of IPTp regimen on STI/RTI risk

During the study period, there were no syndromic diagnoses of C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae ; two participants were diagnosed with symptomatic T. vaginalis and four with BV. At delivery, the prevalence of C. trachomatis , N. gonorrhoeae , T. vaginalis , BV, and GBS colonization at or near delivery in the IPTp-DP arm (reference) was 12.4%, 2.7%, 8.3%, 43.6%, and 11.7%, respectively. Compared with the IPTp-DP arm, the IPTp-SP arm had a markedly lower prevalence of C. trachomatis at delivery [2.5% vs 12.4%; PR = 0.20 (95% CI: 0.12–0.33)], corresponding to NNT  = 10 (95% CI: 8–14) ( Fig. 3 ). Similar reductions were observed when the IPTp-DP arm was compared to the IPTp-DP+SP arm [PR = 0.26 (95% CI: 0.17–0.41)] and the combined IPTp-SP and IPTp-DP+SP arms [PR = 0.23 (95% CI: 0.16–0.33)].

The GBS prevalence was lower among participants randomized to SP-containing IPTp regimens compared to IPTp-DP [8.7% vs 11.7%, any SP: PR = 0.74 (95% CI: 0.53–1.03); NNT = 32 (95% CI: 15–200)], with the largest reduction in the IPTp-SP arm [PR = 0.65 (95% CI: 0.43–0.99); NNT = 24 (95% CI: 13–500)]. The effect sizes for N. gonorrhoeae and T. vaginalis were modest, with wide CIs that included the null. The IPTp effects on BV were attenuated after accounting for the timing of swab collection [PR MI = 1.09 (95% CI: 0.88–1.35) and PR IPSW = 1.09 (95% CI: 0.85–1.40) vs primary estimate PR = 1.17 (95% CI: 1.05–1.30)] ( Supplementary Material Section 4 ). Sensitivity analyses for other STI/RTIs were consistent with the primary results.

### Effect of STIs/RTIs on birth outcomes

In adjusted models, C. trachomatis was associated with a higher risk of preterm delivery [PR = 1.86 (95% CI: 1.07–3.25)] ( Fig. 4 ). The point estimates for N. gonorrhoeae , T. vaginalis , and GBS suggested an increased risk of preterm delivery, but were highly imprecise. For LBW-based outcomes, the associations were generally null and imprecise, except for GBS, which was associated with a 2.08-fold (95% CI: 1.06–4.08) increase in the term-LBW risk and LBW overall [PR = 1.66 (95% CI: 0.94–2.94)]. There was no clear evidence of an association between STIs/RTIs and SGA risk. BV was associated with increased preterm-delivery risk [PR = 1.48 (95% CI: 1.07–2.05)], consistent with the sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Material Section 5 ).

The E-values indicated that, for estimates with 95% CIs that excluded the null, an unmeasured confounder would need to have a PR of ≥2.0 with both the exposure and the outcome, conditional on measured covariates, to fully account for the observed effects ( Fig. 3 ). Sensitivity analyses accounting for the timing of swab collection were consistent with the primary analyses ( Supplementary Material Section 5 ). The preterm-birth estimates (excluding fetal losses) were broadly similar to those for preterm delivery ( Supplementary Material Section 6 ).

### Mediation analyses

Mediation analyses evaluated the extent to which C. trachomatis and GBS contributed to the overall differences in preterm delivery and term LBW between the IPTp arms ( Table 2 ). Compared with IPTp-DP, IPTp-SP was associated with increased preterm-delivery risk [total effect: PR = 1.39 (95% CI: 0.86–2.13)]; however, this effect was partially offset by IPTp-SP’s greater prevention of C. trachomatis [indirect effect: PR = 0.78 (95% CI: 0.57–1.03)]. In contrast, IPTp-SP was associated with lower term-LBW risk compared with IPTp-DP [total effect: PR = 0.28 (95% CI: 0.11–0.56)], which was minimally mediated through GBS prevention [% mediated: 1% (95% CI: –1% to 5%)]. The E-values for indirect effects (1.82 for C. trachomatis and 1.14 for GBS) suggested moderate robustness to unmeasured confounding for the C. trachomatis estimate, but not for GBS.
Discussion:
In this randomized–controlled trial comparing monthly IPTp regimens, the IPTp-SP arm had an 80% lower C. trachomatis prevalence and a 35% lower GBS prevalence at delivery than the IPTp-DP arm. These effects are noteworthy, as C. trachomatis was associated with a 1.86-fold increase in preterm delivery and GBS with a 2.08-fold increase in term LBW. There was no clear evidence to suggest that IPTp-SP influenced N. gonorrhoeae, T. vaginalis , or BV upon correcting for the timing of sample collection. Our results were highly consistent with those of a recent randomized trial that also demonstrated lower C. trachomatis prevalence among women receiving IPTp-SP, but not for N. gonorrhoeae , T. vaginalis , or BV [ 3 ]. We found that BV was associated with increased preterm delivery, consistently with prior meta-analytic evidence [ 35 ]. Collectively, our results suggest that, beyond its antimalarial activity, IPTp-SP may reduce the burden of certain STIs/RTIs, with potential downstream impacts on birth outcomes.

Mediation analyses revealed that, although IPTp-DP had a stronger overall effect than IPTp-SP on reducing preterm birth, likely reflecting its superior antimalarial activity [ 8 , 22 ], the greater impact of IPTp-SP on C. trachomatis partially offset this effect. In contrast, GBS prevention accounted for only a small fraction of the effect of IPTp-SP on term LBW, suggesting the potential involvement of other studied mechanisms, including maternal nutrient absorption [ 36 ], reductions in febrile respiratory illnesses [ 37 ], or the modulation of maternal inflammation [ 38 ]. We also cannot rule out that some of the observed differences reflect the antimalarial or non-malarial effects of IPTp-DP.

In most of sub-Saharan Africa, antenatal STI/RTI screening relies on syndromic management due to limited diagnostic capacity [ 5 ], leading to undertreatment and excess adverse pregnancy outcomes. A modeling study from South Africa estimated that 25.5% of HIV-negative and 34.6% of HIV-positive pregnant women had undiagnosed STIs, for which treatment could have prevented ∼6.3% of preterm deliveries, 10.1% of stillbirths, and 9.1% of LBW infants [ 39 ]. Our findings suggest that IPTp-SP may offer a low-cost chemoprevention strategy against C. trachomatis and GBS, which affected 11%–12% of women in our study and 14%–16% of those in other regions of sub-Saharan Africa [ 40 , 41 ]. Notably, the NNT to prevent one C. trachomatis infection was 10—a compelling figure given its associations with adverse pregnancy and neonatal outcomes [ 42 ]. The 35% reduction in GBS was similarly noteworthy, as GBS is not routinely screened for in resource-limited settings despite its role in neonatal sepsis, morbidity, and mortality [ 43 ]. Thus, even as the antimalarial efficacy of SP declines, its potential STI/RTI-related benefits warrant consideration as continued intervention in addition to more effective malaria-prevention strategies.

Our analysis had limitations. First, most swabs were collected postpartum. However, we do not expect this to have biased our findings, as estimates were highly consistent with those of a recent trial [ 3 ] that evaluated IPTp-SP effects on STIs/RTIs, in which the samples were collected at 32–36 gestational weeks. Moreover, sensitivity analyses, which treated postpartum results as missing and used MI or IPSW, produced estimates that were consistent with the primary results, except for BV, for which the results should be interpreted cautiously. Second, STI/RTI–birth outcome associations and mediation analyses may be subject to unmeasured confounding. However, the E-values suggested that moderately strong unmeasured confounding (RR ≥ 2.0) would be required to fully explain the observed effects. Third, we assessed a limited set of STI/RTI pathogens and the effects on other reproductive tract microbes or pathobionts is unknown. Fourth, we were unable to assess chorioamnionitis or neonatal sepsis, which may be strongly linked to STIs/RTIs. Fifth, we assumed that IPTp-DP had no antibacterial activity. If it does, then the effects of IPTp-SP on STIs/RTIs may have been underestimated. Sixth, STIs/RTIs were not measured at enrollment. Although randomization should have balanced the baseline infection risk across the study arms, the absence of baseline testing prevents distinguishing whether the effects of IPTp-SP reflect the clearance of existing infections or the prevention of incident infections. However, either mechanism is consistent with the chemoprevention role of IPTp-SP. Moreover, assessment of STIs/RTIs at or near delivery may not have fully captured infections during pregnancy, particularly those that would have naturally cleared up by the time of delivery. Lastly, the findings are not generalizable to pregnant women living with HIV, as IPTp-SP is contraindicated for those receiving daily co-trimoxazole, which remains the standard of care in malaria-endemic settings [ 44 ].

The WHO currently recommends IPTp-SP across 34 malaria-endemic African countries despite widespread antifolate resistance [ 1 , 45 ]. Our findings indicate that IPTp-SP reduces C. trachomatis by 80% and GBS by 35%, which could partially explain its positive impacts on newborn outcomes. As alternative IPTp regimens are being considered to replace SP, these ancillary effects should be appreciated, especially in settings with limited STI/RTI screening and treatment.
